content:
GOOGLE PHOTOS RETRIEVAL RESEARCH REPORT
Successful Retrieval of Remembered-But-Imprecisely-Described Photos/Videos
Prepared for: Core Experience team, Google Photos
Analysis basis: 524 DIRECT_RETRIEVAL episodes extracted from 10,641 scanned documents (Play Store, App Store, Reddit, Google Photos community)

====================================================================
1. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
====================================================================

This analysis examines 524 episodes in which a real user tried to retrieve a specific
remembered photo, video, screenshot, or document in Google Photos. It does not evaluate
search quality in the abstract; it traces where, along the chain from "remembering
something happened" to "recognizing the right item on screen," retrieval actually breaks.

Three headline, evidence-backed findings:

- Retrieval breaks down almost equally at three different points, not one. Across the
 524 episodes, the system failing to surface relevant results after a reasonable query
 (SEMANTIC_RETRIEVAL, 138/524 = 26.3%), the user being unable to recognize/confirm the
 right item once in front of a plausible set of candidates (RESULT_EVALUATION, 134/524 =
 25.6%), and the system's organization not matching where the user expects things to be
 (QUERY_UNDERSTANDING, 116/524 = 22.1%) together account for 388/524 (74.0%) of all
 episodes. By contrast, users being unable to express or formulate what they remember at
 all is rare (MEMORY_EXPRESSION + QUERY_FORMULATION = 24/524 = 4.6%). This means the
 primary opportunity is not "help people describe memories better" -- it is fixing what
 happens after a reasonable attempt is made.

- What people forget is disproportionately about the app's own organization, not about
 the photo itself. Using an inferred clustering of the (inconsistent, free-text) forgotten
 category tags, the single largest cluster is not "exact date" (98/524 episodes, 18.7%)
 but the item's location or label inside Google Photos' own structure -- folder, tab,
 archive, storage bucket (144/524 = 27.5%) -- closely trailed by not remembering the
 photo's visual content itself (174/524 = 33.2%). A specific, well-evidenced sub-pattern
 of this is app-generated ephemeral content (collages, cinematic memories, stylized
 photos, "movies," highlights) that the user only ever saw via a push notification and
 then could never relocate: 45/524 episodes (8.6%) fit this pattern, and it resolves in
 the user's favor far less often than the corpus average (NOT_FOUND in 39/45 = 86.7% of
 these episodes vs. 71.0% corpus-wide).

- When it fails, the near-universal fallback is manual visual scanning, not query
 refinement. Only 13/524 episodes (2.5%) show the user deliberately reformulating a
 query (synonym, broadened terms); by contrast, 54/524 episodes (10.3%) record
 MANUAL_SCROLL, TIMELINE_SCROLLING, or ALBUM_BROWSING as the workaround, and 408/524
 (77.9%) of all episodes never get past a single action before the episode ends. This
 is a strong signal that most users do not iterate on search at all -- they either accept
 the first result (or lack of one) or abandon it for brute-force scrolling.

This dataset is best classified as HYPOTHESIS-GENERATING, not conclusively directional
(see Section 2). All quantification below is expressed as count/denominator/% within
this 524-episode sample and must not be read as a population-level success or failure
rate for Google Photos users generally.

====================================================================
2. DATASET QUALITY AND LIMITATIONS
====================================================================

Scale and relevance filtering (aggregated_statistics, exact, corpus-wide):
- 10,641 total documents scanned.
- Relevance classification: DIRECT_RETRIEVAL 2,779 (26.1%), ADJACENT_RETRIEVAL 2,615
 (24.6%), NOT_RELEVANT 4,019 (37.8%), UNCERTAIN 318 (3.0%). These four figures sum to
 9,731, not 10,641 -- a gap of 910 documents (8.6% of the corpus) not accounted for in
 the distribution provided. This gap is unexplained by the data given and is flagged as
 UNKNOWN (see Section 9); it is a data-completeness irregularity, not something we can
 resolve here.
- Per the task's scope rules, ADJACENT_RETRIEVAL (backup/sync/deletion problems) is
 explicitly NOT retrieval-failure evidence and is excluded from findings; NOT_RELEVANT
 and UNCERTAIN are excluded entirely.
- 524 episodes were extracted from DIRECT_RETRIEVAL-classified documents. 524 divided
 into 2,779 DIRECT_RETRIEVAL documents is only 18.9% -- most DIRECT_RETRIEVAL documents
 did not yield an analyzable episode in this set, for reasons not stated in the data
 (UNKNOWN).

Source representation -- a major, load-bearing limitation:
- At the document level (corpus-wide), sources are: play_store 8,705 (81.8%), reddit
 1,847 (17.4%), app_store 58 (0.5%), google_photos_community 31 (0.3%).
- At the episode level (the 524 analyzed episodes), every single episode_id/
 source_document_id is prefixed "playstore_us_" -- i.e., 524/524 (100%) of episodes in
 this sample come from Play Store reviews. Zero Reddit, App Store, or community-forum
 episodes are present in the episode set, despite Reddit alone representing 17.4% of
 documents and being a channel known for longer, more narrative posts. This is the
 single biggest constraint on this analysis: everything below describes patterns in
 short-form, complaint-oriented Play Store reviews, not the full range of channels in
 which people describe searching for a remembered photo.
- Play Store reviews are structurally biased toward complaints (people who are frustrated
 are more likely to leave a review than people whose search worked). Corpus-wide,
 NOT_FOUND (372/524 = 71.0%) and ABANDONED (47/524 = 9.0%) together account for 80.0%
 of outcomes, while FOUND_DIRECTLY is only 26/524 (5.0%). This ratio almost certainly
 understates real-world success rate and must never be read as "80% of Google Photos
 searches fail."

Scenario-label reliability:
- The scenario field is noisy. OTHER (253/524 = 48.3%) and UNKNOWN (84/524 = 16.0%)
 together account for 64.3% of episodes and carry no specific life context.
- The WORK label (52/524 = 9.9%) does NOT mean "photos related to a job," on direct
 inspection of scenario_description text for all 52 WORK-labeled episodes (e.g. "User
 unable to find device folders after UI redesign," "User cannot find edited photos after
 they disappear from albums," "User's photos are mis-grouped by face recognition despite
 being manually named"). None of the sampled WORK descriptions concern occupational
 photo use; they are near-uniformly about in-app reorganization/navigation friction. This
 is a labeling artifact we treat as KNOWN (directly verified by reading the underlying
 text) and we do not use "WORK" as a real behavioral segment; we use it only as a proxy
 for "reorganization-driven complaint," flagged as such throughout.
- Combining OTHER + UNKNOWN + WORK, 389/524 (74.2%) of episodes carry a generic or
 mislabeled scenario tag. Only 135/524 (25.8%) carry a specific, interpretable life
 context (FAMILY 32, HOBBY 33, FRIENDS 19, TRAVEL 10, PET 10, SCREENSHOT 10, DOCUMENT 7,
 HOME 6, EVENT 4, SHOPPING 3, RECEIPT 1). Scenario-level conclusions (Q10, Section 6)
 are therefore lower-confidence than stage-level conclusions.

Field completeness:
- remembered{} is empty in 83/524 episodes (15.8%) -- no evidence of what, if anything,
 the user consciously recalled.
- forgotten[] is empty in 113/524 episodes (21.6%).
- Both are empty in 36/524 episodes (6.9%).
- Of 354 SEARCH actions recorded across all journeys, only 73 (20.6%) have a captured
 query string; 79.4% show query=null, meaning the actual words the user typed are
 usually not recoverable from the source text.
- Of NOT_FOUND episodes (372), 353 (94.9%) show no recorded workaround. We cannot tell
 whether these users truly took no further action, silently tried something the review
 text didn't mention, or the workaround simply wasn't captured by the extraction step.

Corpus classification: B. HYPOTHESIS-GENERATING ONLY.
Rationale (2-4 sentences): The sample is large enough (524 episodes) to detect recurring
mechanisms and produce credible, quotable evidence, and the failure-stage and workaround
distributions are internally consistent between the aggregated statistics and the
episode-level data we independently recomputed (exact match). However, 100% single-channel
sourcing (Play Store only, despite Reddit being a real and different channel),
complaint-review selection bias, and 74% generic/mislabeled scenario tags mean this
dataset can surface credible mechanisms and rank candidate problems, but cannot establish
true prevalence, true success rate, or segment-level population estimates. Treat every
finding below as a hypothesis to validate, not a confirmed root cause.

====================================================================
3. ANSWERS TO THE DISCOVERY QUESTIONS
====================================================================

Q1. What kinds of old photos, videos, screenshots, or documents do users struggle to
retrieve?
Pattern: The large majority of episodes concern ordinary photos, not other media types.
target_type distribution (524/524, exact): PHOTO 458 (87.4%), VIDEO 35 (6.7%), OTHER 16
(3.1%), SCREENSHOT 13 (2.5%), DOCUMENT 2 (0.4%).
A distinct, well-evidenced sub-pattern cuts across scenarios: app-generated ephemeral
content (collages, "cinematic memories," stylized photos, auto-made "movies," highlights)
that the user saw once via a push notification and then could not relocate: 45/524
episodes (8.6%) match this pattern by keyword (collage/animation/stylized/highlight/
cinematic/movie/montage/creation), and it fails (NOT_FOUND) at 39/45 (86.7%), well above
the corpus baseline of 71.0%. Example episode_ids: playstore_us_0daace25 (cinematic
memory), playstore_us_12f40d3f (collage after update), playstore_us_d954fa4a (saved
collage disappears), playstore_us_bda6d2e2 (stylized panoramas), playstore_us_9c15f415
("For You" section removed, animations/montages gone).
Confidence: HIGH for target_type distribution (exact, aggregated + independently
recomputed). MEDIUM for the ephemeral-content sub-pattern (keyword-matched, INFERRED
grouping, but large and consistent effect size).

Q2. What information do people actually remember about a photo when they start
searching?
Pattern: The dominant remembered dimension is diffuse situational "context," not concrete
visual descriptors. memoryDimensionFrequency (share of 524 episodes mentioning each
dimension, exact aggregated count): context 305 (58.2%), activities 179 (34.2%), time 156
(29.8%), people 36 (6.9%), objects 36 (6.9%), relationships 36 (6.9%), events 24 (4.6%),
visualAttributes 23 (4.4%), places 10 (1.9%), textInImage 6 (1.1%). 83/524 (15.8%)
episodes show no remembered content at all.
A meaningful outcome contrast (computed from episode data): among FOUND_DIRECTLY episodes
(n=26), "objects" appears in 9 (34.6%) and the average number of remembered dimensions
is 2.00; among NOT_FOUND episodes (n=372), "objects" appears in only 18 (4.8%) and the
average is 1.59. Illustrative FOUND_DIRECTLY queries that succeeded: "truck," "cabinet,"
"passport," "mountains," "cocoa" (text-in-image), "person A person B dog." This suggests
-- but does not prove -- that remembering a concrete, nameable object or subject
correlates with successful direct retrieval more than remembering only situational
context or activity.
Confidence: MEDIUM. This is a correlational pattern from a self-selected, complaint-
biased sample; Section 8 (contradictions) shows counter-examples where concrete-object
queries also failed.
Evidence episode_ids: playstore_us_1bfd4fad, /ep1,
playstore_us_b7c27524, playstore_us_e7f24415,.

Q3. What information have they forgotten by the time they search?
Pattern: forgotten[] tags are free text with 276 distinct values across 627 total
mentions in 524 episodes -- the underlying taxonomy is inconsistent (INFERRED clustering
was required; treat cluster boundaries as approximate, not exact). Clustering by keyword
yields (episodes with at least one tag in the cluster; a tag can match >1 cluster):
- Visual content / what the item actually shows: 174/524 (33.2%)
- Location within the app itself (folder/tab/archive/storage -- not geographic place):
 144/524 (27.5%)
- Which exact item among several similar candidates: 108/524 (20.6%)
- Exact date/time: 98/524 (18.7%)
- Who is in it / person identity: 66/524 (12.6%)
- Which album / album name: 37/524 (7.1%)
- Organizational structure generally: 20/524 (3.8%)
- What search term/keyword to use: 9/524 (1.7%)
Contrary to a common assumption, "forgot the exact date" (18.7%) is not the largest
forgotten category -- not knowing the app's own current organization/location (27.5%) is
larger, and not remembering the visual content itself (33.2%) is larger still.
Confidence: MEDIUM (clustering is inferred over an inconsistent free-text taxonomy of
unknown upstream reliability).

Q4. How do users formulate a search when their memory is incomplete?
Pattern: Most attempts are short and are never observed to be refined. Of 354 SEARCH
actions across all journeys, 281 (79.4%) have no captured query text. Among the 73 with
captured text, most are 1-3 word noun phrases naming a concrete subject ("truck,"
"cabinet," "passport," "mountains," "rain," "water rail," "Amp," "cat or dog") rather than
descriptive sentences; one clear exception fully described a scene and succeeded ("picture
of myself and my wife sitting in front of some tulips about 5 years ago," FOUND_DIRECTLY).
408/524 episodes (77.9%) show a search_journey of exactly one action -- most commonly
SEARCH (249), BROWSE_TIMELINE (69), OPEN_ALBUM (35), MANUAL_SCROLL (29), or FILTER_DATE
(13) -- meaning most episodes never show a second attempt in any direction.
Confidence: MEDIUM (query-text capture is sparse; conclusions rest on the 20.6% of
SEARCH actions with visible text, plus the action-type tallies which are exact).

Q5. How do users reformulate their search after an initial attempt fails?
Pattern: Deliberate reformulation is rare. Only 13/524 episodes (2.5%) contain any
reformulation-type action (REFORMULATE, TRY_SYNONYM, BROADEN_QUERY/SEARCH) anywhere in
the journey. The specific two-step chain SEARCH -> REFORMULATE occurs 6 times and
succeeds (FOUND_AFTER_REFORMULATION) in 4/6 (66.7%) -- the best conversion rate of any
multi-step chain, but on a tiny base. Far more common than query reformulation is
abandoning search for a structurally different action: SEARCH -> MANUAL_SCROLL (19
episodes, bigram count), SEARCH -> OPEN_ALBUM (10), SEARCH -> BROWSE_TIMELINE (9),
SEARCH -> SEARCH (11, i.e., repeating the identical action rather than varying it).
Confidence: MEDIUM-HIGH (exact action-sequence tallies across all 524 episodes).
Evidence: playstore_us_cba74328 (reformulated from "text in image" to remembered text,
succeeded), playstore_us_638655a9 ("Amp" stopped working, had to try "Speaker").

Q6. Does Google Photos fail to understand the clues the user does provide?
Pattern: Yes, in two distinguishable ways, both well evidenced. (a) QUERY_UNDERSTANDING
failures (116/524 = 22.1%) are overwhelmingly about the system's organizational scheme,
not literal keyword matching: album names are not searchable (playstore_us_20031183: "no
way to... search for the name of the album"), folders/tabs got relabeled after a redesign
(playstore_us_ca22fd58), shared/partner content stopped surfacing (playstore_us_6398980d).
(b) SEMANTIC_RETRIEVAL failures (138/524 = 26.3%, the single largest stage) show direct
vocabulary/label mismatch: a photo labeled "water rail" (a bird) returns river-adjacent
train photos instead; searching "rain" returns nothing despite
"thousands of rain photos" (playstore_us_e0c3dbc6); searching a known contact's name no
longer returns their photos (playstore_us_00b602a7). 17/524 episodes (3.2%) explicitly
attribute a regression to "the new AI search" or "Gemini."
Confidence: HIGH for stage-level counts (exact, cross-validated against aggregated
statistics). HIGH for the qualitative pattern (many concrete, specific quotes).

Q7. Are potentially relevant results difficult for the user to evaluate or recognize?
Pattern: Yes -- RESULT_EVALUATION is the second-largest failure stage (134/524 = 25.6%).
Representative causes: photos misdated/scattered across the wrong years, stacked/grouped photos hiding the
target until manually "unstacked" (playstore_us_75c014f1), a visual bug rendering photos
as black screens (playstore_us_4a7ee0b1), and albums reporting "1 photo added" while the
photo never visibly appears (playstore_us_ebe3aa3d). This friction is concentrated after
the user has already navigated to a plausible location: episodes whose entire journey is
just OPEN_ALBUM (35 episodes) show RESULT_EVALUATION as the failure stage in 21/35 (60%)
-- i.e., once inside an album, recognizing/confirming the item, not finding the album, is
the actual blocker.
Confidence: MEDIUM-HIGH.

Q8. What workarounds do users fall back on after a search fails?
Pattern: No workaround is recorded in 417/524 episodes (79.6%). Among the 107 episodes
with one: MANUAL_SCROLL 25 (4.8%), TIMELINE_SCROLLING 18 (3.4%), ALBUM_BROWSING 11
(2.1%), USE_EXTERNAL_SEARCH 9 (1.7%), GIVE_UP 6 (1.1%), DATE_FILTERING 6 (1.1%),
TRY_SYNONYMS 5 (1.0%), CHECK_DEVICE 5 (1.0%), remaining categories at or below 4 each.
Combined manual-scanning workarounds (MANUAL_SCROLL + TIMELINE_SCROLLING +
ALBUM_BROWSING) total 54/524 (10.3%) and outnumber all deliberate query-refinement
workarounds (TRY_SYNONYMS + DATE_FILTERING = 11/524, 2.1%) by roughly 5 to 1.
Among NOT_FOUND outcomes specifically (n=372), 353 (94.9%) show no recorded workaround,
so we do not know whether these are true dead-ends or under-captured.
Confidence: HIGH for the exact counts; the interpretation of "no workaround" is UNKNOWN.

Q9. At which stage does retrieval most often break down?
Pattern: Excluding NONE (28/524, 5.3%, episodes with no failure), the ranking of the 496
episodes that did break down is: SEMANTIC_RETRIEVAL 138 (27.8% of failures),
RESULT_EVALUATION 134 (27.0%), QUERY_UNDERSTANDING 116 (23.4%), RECOVERY 84 (16.9%),
QUERY_FORMULATION 15 (3.0%), MEMORY_EXPRESSION 9 (1.8%). The top three stages
(SEMANTIC_RETRIEVAL, RESULT_EVALUATION, QUERY_UNDERSTANDING) account for 388/524 (74.0%)
of all episodes and 388/496 (78.2%) of all failures. The earliest stages in the funnel
(can the user express/formulate what they remember at all) are the rarest failure points
by a wide margin.
Confidence: HIGH (exact, cross-validated against aggregated_statistics.failureStageDistribution).

Q10. How do these behaviors differ across scenarios?
Pattern: Distinct, but confidence varies sharply with sample size per scenario (see
Section 2's scenario-label caveat and Section 6's matrix). Headline contrasts:
- WORK-labeled episodes (n=52, best read as "reorganization/redesign complaints," not
 occupational context -- see Section 2) show QUERY_UNDERSTANDING in 30/52 (57.7%), by
 far the most concentrated single stage-in-scenario result in the whole matrix, well
 above the 22.1% corpus rate.
- UNKNOWN-scenario episodes (n=84, thin metadata) show RECOVERY in 40/84 (47.6%), also
 far above the corpus rate of 16.0%; these episodes tend to be short, low-detail
 complaints ("can't find anything anymore") that don't specify what's being searched for.
- FAMILY episodes (n=32) skew toward SEMANTIC_RETRIEVAL (11/32 = 34.4%) and include a
 distinct emotionally high-stakes sub-pattern: searching for photos/videos of a deceased
 family member or pet (7 episodes identified across FAMILY/PET scenarios; see
 hypothesis H5 in Section 7).
- HOBBY episodes (n=33) show QUERY_UNDERSTANDING leading (10/33 = 30.3%) and disproportionately
 contain the auto-generated-content pattern from Q1.
- OTHER (n=253, largest bucket but least specific) is led by RESULT_EVALUATION (92/253 =
 36.4%) then SEMANTIC_RETRIEVAL (70/253 = 27.7%).
- Scenarios with n<15 (TRAVEL 10, PET 10, SCREENSHOT 10, DOCUMENT 7, HOME 6, EVENT 4,
 SHOPPING 3, RECEIPT 1) show directionally interesting splits (e.g., DOCUMENT is 5/7 =
 71% SEMANTIC_RETRIEVAL) but are flagged INSUFFICIENT/LOW confidence given sample size.
Confidence: MEDIUM for n>=30 scenario rows, LOW/INSUFFICIENT below that.

====================================================================
4. FAILURE-STAGE DECOMPOSITION
====================================================================

Chain: MEMORY_EXPRESSION -> QUERY_FORMULATION -> QUERY_UNDERSTANDING ->
SEMANTIC_RETRIEVAL -> RESULT_EVALUATION -> RECOVERY

MEMORY_EXPRESSION -- 9/524 (1.7%)
The user cannot articulate what they remember at all, distinct from struggling to turn a
clear memory into a query. Rarest stage. Representative: playstore_us_9b9885db ("Instead
looking at every photo... find a photo in sec instead of hrs" -- no describable memory
offered), playstore_us_a69ee60c (notification-only content the user can't otherwise
characterize). Scenarios: scattered (OTHER, UNKNOWN, WORK, HOBBY, FRIENDS, one each).
Confidence: LOW-MEDIUM given n=9; too small to segment further.

QUERY_FORMULATION -- 15/524 (2.9%)
The user has a memory but struggles to turn it into an actionable query/action (e.g.,
wants to tag a known face but the mechanism to search by it doesn't exist).
Representative: playstore_us_6ada2c18 ("I know who it is and I want to be able to tag and
find that picture that contains them" -- ABANDONED), playstore_us_31ef4ea5 (knows the
source -- WhatsApp -- but no way to query by it). Concentrated somewhat in FAMILY (4/32)
and HOBBY (2/33). Confidence: MEDIUM.

QUERY_UNDERSTANDING -- 116/524 (22.1%)
The system doesn't map the user's stated clues onto its own structure. Heavily
concentrated in WORK-labeled/reorganization episodes (30/52 = 57.7% of that scenario) and
recurs in album-name search, folder/tab relabeling, and shared-content relocation.
Representative: playstore_us_a6ece435, playstore_us_ca22fd58, playstore_us_20031183.
Confidence: HIGH (large n, concentrated, very concrete quotes).

SEMANTIC_RETRIEVAL -- 138/524 (26.3%), the single largest stage
Query is reasonable, results don't surface. Representative: 
("water rail" -> train photos), playstore_us_e0c3dbc6 ("rain" -> nothing despite
thousands), playstore_us_638655a9 ("Amp" -> nothing, "Speaker" worked). 17/524 (3.2%)
explicitly blame an "AI"/"Gemini" search change. Confidence: HIGH.

RESULT_EVALUATION -- 134/524 (25.6%)
Results/candidates are in front of the user but can't be confirmed as the right item.
Representative: (misdated photos), playstore_us_75c014f1
(stacked photos hiding target), playstore_us_4a7ee0b1 (black-screen display bug).
Disproportionately follows OPEN_ALBUM-only journeys (21/35 = 60%). Confidence:
MEDIUM-HIGH (some quotes blend recognition friction with app reliability bugs -- see
Section 8).

RECOVERY -- 84/524 (16.0%)
An initial attempt failed and a second attempt (often unspecified) also fails.
Disproportionately concentrated in the thin-metadata UNKNOWN scenario (40/84 = 47.6% of
all RECOVERY cases come from UNKNOWN-scenario episodes alone), which limits how precisely
we can characterize this stage: we mostly know a second attempt failed, not what was
tried. Representative: playstore_us_8ceb5848 (uploaded video vanished), playstore_us_fa03a662
(deceased father's photos, folder relocated). Confidence: MEDIUM (large n but low
specificity in the dominant sub-segment).

NONE -- 28/524 (5.3%)
No failure; included for completeness as the success baseline against which the above
percentages are best read.

====================================================================
5. RECURRING BEHAVIORAL CHAINS
====================================================================

Chains are derived directly from the search_journey field across all 524 episodes.
"Success" below = FOUND_DIRECTLY + FOUND_AFTER_WORKAROUND + FOUND_AFTER_REFORMULATION.

1. SEARCH (single action, no follow-up) -- 249/524 episodes (47.5%), the most common
 pattern by far. Outcomes: NOT_FOUND 212 (85.1%), ABANDONED 16 (6.4%), success 20
 (8.0%: FOUND_DIRECTLY 10, FOUND_AFTER_WORKAROUND 7, FOUND_AFTER_REFORMULATION 3).
 Dominant failure stage: SEMANTIC_RETRIEVAL (80/249 = 32.1%). Top scenarios: OTHER
 (106), UNKNOWN (42), WORK (27). Typical workaround: none. Confidence: HIGH (n=249).

2. BROWSE_TIMELINE (single action) -- 69/524 (13.2%). Outcomes: NOT_FOUND 52 (75.4%),
 ABANDONED 8 (11.6%), success 9 (13.0%). Dominant failure stage: RESULT_EVALUATION
 (27/69 = 39.1%). Top scenarios: OTHER (30), WORK (16, 23.2% of this chain). Reading:
 users who go straight to chronological scrolling, skipping search entirely, often
 because a redesign broke their prior mental model (over-indexed in WORK-labeled
 episodes). Confidence: HIGH.

3. OPEN_ALBUM (single action) -- 35/524 (6.7%). Outcomes: NOT_FOUND 29 (82.9%), success 4
 (11.4%). Dominant failure stage: RESULT_EVALUATION (21/35 = 60.0%). Reading: users who
 go directly to an album (bypassing search) but then can't recognize the target item
 within it. Confidence: MEDIUM-HIGH.

4. MANUAL_SCROLL (single action, last resort) -- 29/524 (5.5%). Outcomes:
 FOUND_AFTER_WORKAROUND 12 (41.4%), NOT_FOUND 8 (27.6%), ABANDONED 9 (31.0%). This is
 the highest single-action success rate of any chain (41.4%), but a third of users
 abandon mid-scroll, and successful cases cite real time cost ("scroll for 30+ min,"
 playstore_us_eaaf5390). Confidence: MEDIUM (n=29).

5. SEARCH -> MANUAL_SCROLL -- 19/524 (3.6%). Outcomes: FOUND_AFTER_WORKAROUND 9,
 FOUND_AFTER_REFORMULATION 1, NOT_FOUND 6, ABANDONED 3. Success rate 52.6% -- the best
 success rate of any chain with n>=15, better than SEARCH alone (8.0%) or
 BROWSE_TIMELINE alone (13.0%). Reading: search narrows the space even when it doesn't
 return the exact item, and a manual scan on top of it is disproportionately effective
 -- at the cost of user time. Confidence: MEDIUM-HIGH.

6. FILTER_DATE (single action) -- 13/524 (2.5%). Outcomes: NOT_FOUND 10 (76.9%), success
 2 (15.4%). Notable because date-filtering is the intuitively "correct" workaround for
 users who forgot the exact date, yet it still fails most of the time -- consistent
 with the RESULT_EVALUATION evidence of misdated/scrambled timelines (Section 4).
 Confidence: MEDIUM (n=13).

7. SEARCH -> REFORMULATE -- 6/524 (1.1%). Outcomes: FOUND_AFTER_REFORMULATION 4 (66.7%),
 NOT_FOUND 2. Best conversion rate of any 2-step chain, but the rarest strategy overall
 (Q5). Confidence: LOW (n=6) but directionally consistent with Q5.

8. SEARCH -> SEARCH (identical repeated action) -- 7/524 (1.3%) bigram-level; 11/524
 (2.1%) at the "SEARCH, OTHER" adjacency level. Reading: a nontrivial share of users
 repeat the same search rather than varying it, suggesting either persistence-without-
 iteration or uncertainty about how to change the query. Confidence: LOW-MEDIUM.

====================================================================
6. SCENARIO x FAILURE-STAGE MATRIX
====================================================================

Format per scenario: n = episode count; dominant failure stage(s) with % of that
scenario's episodes; WORKAROUND_FRICTION = % of that scenario's episodes with no
recorded workaround (a proxy for "users have no visible fallback"); EVIDENCE_CONFIDENCE
per Section 2's sample-size caveat.

OTHER (n=253, 48.3% of corpus -- generic, low scenario-specificity)
 RESULT_EVALUATION 92 (36.4%), SEMANTIC_RETRIEVAL 70 (27.7%), QUERY_UNDERSTANDING 39
 (15.4%), RECOVERY 28 (11.1%). WORKAROUND_FRICTION: 76% no workaround. EVIDENCE_VOLUME:
 HIGH. EVIDENCE_CONFIDENCE: MEDIUM (large n, but "OTHER" is a catch-all so causal
 interpretation is weaker).

UNKNOWN (n=84, thin metadata)
 RECOVERY 40 (47.6%), RESULT_EVALUATION 15 (17.9%), SEMANTIC_RETRIEVAL 14 (16.7%),
 QUERY_UNDERSTANDING 11 (13.1%). WORKAROUND_FRICTION: 81% no workaround.
 EVIDENCE_VOLUME: MEDIUM-HIGH. EVIDENCE_CONFIDENCE: LOW (scenario itself means "we don't
 know the context"; RECOVERY dominance may just mean these are the vaguest complaints).

7. RANKED OPPORTUNITY HYPOTHESES (TOP 5)
====================================================================

An opportunity is a user outcome, not a feature. Priority is reasoned qualitatively from
evidence volume x failure severity x addressability, not a computed score.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
HYPOTHESIS 1

OPPORTUNITY: Help users successfully retrieve a photo, video, or collage that Google
Photos itself auto-generated (a "memory," collage, cinematic clip, stylized photo, or
highlight) when they remember that it was created and roughly when/why, but have
forgotten where it lives once the originating push notification is gone, because the
app currently does not give these creations a stable, browsable home, which causes them
to be effectively lost after the notification disappears.

TARGET SEGMENT/SCENARIO: Cross-cuts HOBBY, EVENT, WORK-labeled, and OTHER scenarios;
defined by content type (app-generated ephemeral creations) rather than a single life
scenario.

WHAT USERS REMEMBER: That the creation exists and that a notification introduced it
(context, activities dimensions -- e.g., "auto-generated," "received notifications,"
"suggested by app").

WHAT USERS HAVE FORGOTTEN: The current location/label of the creation inside the app's
structure (not its visual content -- they usually still know exactly what it looked
like).

PRIMARY FAILURE STAGE: Mixed but concentrated in RESULT_EVALUATION (14/45) and
QUERY_UNDERSTANDING (14/45), with RECOVERY (7/45) next.

CURRENT WORKAROUND: Overwhelmingly none; a few resort to re-triggering the notification
or checking a shared album.

EVIDENCE: 45/524 episodes (8.6%) match this pattern by keyword; NOT_FOUND in 39/45
(86.7%) vs. 71.0% corpus-wide. episode_ids: playstore_us_0daace25, playstore_us_12f40d3f,
playstore_us_a6ece435, playstore_us_f5fd3a8f, playstore_us_696c04fc, playstore_us_57fd0a5a,
playstore_us_2911201a,, playstore_us_d954fa4a,
, playstore_us_bda6d2e2, playstore_us_00629ae7,
, playstore_us_7ca957a7, playstore_us_4f0fe129,
playstore_us_edb70feb, playstore_us_3ed4159c, playstore_us_9c15f415. Source: 100% Play
Store (see Section 2 caveat).

WORKAROUND FRICTION: HIGH (86.7% NOT_FOUND, near-total absence of any recorded
workaround).

WHY IT MATTERS TO SUCCESSFUL RETRIEVAL: These are items the user knows exist and can
describe precisely (unlike most other episodes), yet the failure rate is the highest of
any pattern identified. If "remember it, can't find it" retrieval failures have a
best-case segment to fix, this is a strong candidate: memory is not the bottleneck here,
system information architecture is.

KNOWN: 45 episodes explicitly describe this pattern; NOT_FOUND rate is 15.7 percentage
points above corpus baseline. INFERRED: that this is caused by a specific IA gap (no
persistent "creations" surface) rather than, e.g., users simply not looking hard enough.
UNKNOWN: true frequency in the full user population; whether a stable surface for these
creations already exists but is undiscoverable, or genuinely does not exist.

EVIDENCE CONFIDENCE: MEDIUM-HIGH (large, consistent, keyword-matched pattern; single-
channel source).

PRIORITY: P1 -- largest, most internally consistent effect size of any candidate
identified, with a distinctly higher failure rate than baseline.

PRIMARY RESEARCH QUESTION: When a user is shown their own generated collage/animation/
memory today, can they find it again unaided a week later, and if not, where do they

HYPOTHESIS 2

OPPORTUNITY: Help users successfully retrieve a photo when they remember a concrete,
nameable subject (an object, place, or person) and enter that word or name as a search

FAMILY, HOBBY. Defined by query behavior (a single, concrete-subject SEARCH action) more

WHAT USERS REMEMBER: A concrete subject -- object, place, or person's name (the
"objects," "people," or "textInImage" remembered dimensions).

WHAT USERS HAVE FORGOTTEN: Often nothing specific; this is a case where clue expression

PRIMARY FAILURE STAGE: SEMANTIC_RETRIEVAL, 138/524 (26.3%), the single largest stage
corpus-wide.

CURRENT WORKAROUND: Mostly none (this stage's episodes are dominated by the SEARCH-only

playstore_us_638655a9 ("Amp" broke, "Speaker" worked), playstore_us_00b602a7 (contact-name

/ep1 ("someone in white"/"someone in black" both failed).

WORKAROUND FRICTION: HIGH (SEARCH-alone chain succeeds only 8.0% of the time).

WHY IT MATTERS TO SUCCESSFUL RETRIEVAL: This is the largest single failure stage in the

KNOWN: stage size and many concrete literal-mismatch examples. INFERRED: that a
"vocabulary/label mismatch" mechanism, rather than a general system reliability issue,

aggregated statistics).

PRIORITY: P1.

PRIMARY RESEARCH QUESTION: When a user's concrete-subject search fails, is the target
photo actually indexed/labeled with a matching term at all, and if so, why didn't it
surface -- ranking, recency, or literal term mismatch?

HYPOTHESIS 3

OPPORTUNITY: Help users who know an item exists and roughly what it's about, but have
lost track of where Google Photos currently organizes it after an app redesign or

preserve or clearly communicate the user's prior mental model of where things live,
which causes them to conclude items are missing even when they are not.

TARGET SEGMENT/SCENARIO: The reorganization-complaint proxy segment (labeled WORK in the

WHAT USERS REMEMBER: That items were organized a certain way before (albums, folders,
"For You" tab, people/pets grouping) -- context and activities dimensions.

WHAT USERS HAVE FORGOTTEN: The current location/label/structure after a change they may
not have been aware of.

PRIMARY FAILURE STAGE: QUERY_UNDERSTANDING, 116/524 overall (22.1%); 30/52 (57.7%) within
the WORK-labeled subset specifically -- the single most concentrated scenario-stage cell

CURRENT WORKAROUND: Mostly none (90% of WORK-labeled episodes record no workaround);
where present, BROWSE_TIMELINE (manual chronological scroll) is the most common fallback.

EVIDENCE: episode_ids: playstore_us_a6ece435, playstore_us_ca22fd58, playstore_us_20031183,
playstore_us_6398980d, playstore_us_9c15f415, playstore_us_8261cfbc, playstore_us_77db3970,
playstore_us_f3263900. WORK-labeled outcomes: 94% NOT_FOUND or ABANDONED, the worst
resolution rate of any scenario with n>=10.

WORKAROUND FRICTION: HIGH (90% no workaround, 94% unresolved).

WHY IT MATTERS TO SUCCESSFUL RETRIEVAL: This is the segment with the worst resolution

KNOWN: concentration and resolution-rate figures are exact and internally consistent.
INFERRED: that redesign/reorganization is the causal trigger (the evidence text
repeatedly says so, but we cannot confirm from this data which specific releases or
changes are implicated). UNKNOWN: whether affected users eventually adapt to a new
structure over time (this dataset only captures the complaint moment, not resolution

EVIDENCE CONFIDENCE: HIGH.

PRIORITY: P1 (tied with H1/H2 on evidence strength; kept as P1/P2 boundary because part
of its severity is attributable to a labeling proxy rather than a directly-confirmed
segment -- validate the WORK-as-reorg-proxy reading before treating this as fully

PRIMARY RESEARCH QUESTION: After a Google Photos redesign, how long does it take affected

anything, would have preserved continuity for them?

WHAT USERS REMEMBER: The person or pet (people/relationships dimensions), frequently a

WHAT USERS HAVE FORGOTTEN: The current location of the people/pets folder or face group,

CURRENT WORKAROUND: Mostly none.

KNOWN: the 7 episodes and their outcomes as quoted. INFERRED: that this is mechanistically

====================================================================
8. CONTRADICTORY EVIDENCE
====================================================================

Contradiction to H1 (auto-generated content is unrecoverable): A small minority of the
45 matched episodes did resolve successfully (FOUND_DIRECTLY 2, FOUND_AFTER_WORKAROUND 2,
FOUND_AFTER_REFORMULATION 1 -- 5/45, 11.1%), showing the content is not universally
unrecoverable; some users do relocate it, typically via search or a shared album check
(playstore_us_2911201a, workaround CHECK_SHARED_ALBUM). Impact on confidence: moderate --
does not undermine the core pattern (86.7% NOT_FOUND is still far above baseline) but
means "unrecoverable" should be softened to "unreliably recoverable."

Contradiction to H2 (semantic/vocabulary mismatch): Several FOUND_DIRECTLY episodes used
exactly the same style of query (a single concrete noun) that fails elsewhere: "truck"
(playstore_us_1bfd4fad), "cabinet", "mountains", "passport" (playstore_us_e7f24415) all succeeded immediately.
This directly contradicts a blanket claim that concrete-object queries are unreliable;
the failures (rain, water rail, Amp) may reflect specific mislabeling of those particular
photos, indexing lag, or a specific regression window (several "used to work" quotes)
rather than a general property of the search system. Also, 17/524 "AI/Gemini" complaints
are a small, recency-biased subset (3.2%) that may not generalize to the broader
SEMANTIC_RETRIEVAL population. Impact on confidence: meaningful -- suggests H2 should be
scoped as "unreliable, not uniformly broken" and that root-causing needs to separate
indexing/labeling failures from ranking/matching failures, which this dataset cannot do.

Contradiction to H3 (reorganization breaks navigation and it doesn't recover): A
meaningful number of WORK-labeled/reorg episodes do resolve, specifically by switching to
search when browsing fails: playstore_us_7f180581 states directly, "the only way to find
the album is to use the search function" (outcome FOUND_AFTER_REFORMULATION). This
suggests search, not improved browsing/navigation, is sometimes the actual practical fix
for location-amnesia -- which complicates a pure "fix navigation continuity" framing and
suggests search-as-universal-fallback may be a valid design response worth testing
directly against navigation redesign. Also, some WORK-labeled complaints are arguably UI
preference complaints ("bring back the old memories tab") rather than genuine failures to
ever find content again -- this dataset cannot distinguish "never found it" from "found
it eventually but resented the extra effort," since most reviews are captured at the
moment of frustration.

Contradiction to H4 (result-evaluation friction is a recognition/cognition problem):
Several RESULT_EVALUATION quotes describe pure reliability bugs rather than a
memory/recognition difficulty -- e.g., playstore_us_753620a2 ("just so annoying to wait
for them to load") is a performance complaint, not a recognition failure. Mixing
performance/bug-driven RESULT_EVALUATION episodes with genuine "too many similar photos,
can't tell which is right" episodes overstates the size of a pure cognitive-friction
problem. Impact on confidence: reduces confidence that a single UX fix addresses this
whole 134-episode stage; at least two distinct mechanisms (bugs vs. cognitive load) are
present.

Contradiction to H5 (grief-related retrieval is broken): Two of the seven identified
episodes resolved successfully via ordinary search (playstore_us_b7c27524: "searched a
place or his name & up they all popped," FOUND_DIRECTLY; playstore_us_7baf1f03: also
FOUND_DIRECTLY). This shows the underlying retrieval mechanism is not inherently broken
for this segment, and that failures correlate more with the same face/folder-relocation
mechanism as H3 than with anything unique to grief-related search. Impact: suggests H5 is
better framed as a severity-weighted instance of H3, not an independent root cause,
pending further validation -- it still deserves separate attention because of the
disproportionate emotional cost of failure, but should not be pursued as a technically
distinct problem from H3 without more evidence.

Contradiction to the chain-level finding "manual scrolling works better than search
alone" (Section 5, item 4/5): the higher success rate of MANUAL_SCROLL (41.4%) and
SEARCH->MANUAL_SCROLL (52.6%) vs. SEARCH alone (8.0%) is very plausibly a selection
effect, not evidence that scrolling is inherently a better retrieval mechanism: users
resort to full manual scrolling largely when they are highly confident the item exists
and are willing to invest significant time, which mechanically raises the success rate
for that subgroup regardless of the workaround's intrinsic effectiveness. This
substantially weakens any recommendation framed as "make scrolling easier" without also
accounting for the large time cost these same quotes describe (e.g., "scroll for 30+
min").

====================================================================
9. KNOWN VS. INFERRED VS. UNKNOWN
====================================================================

WHAT THE DATA SUPPORTS (KNOWN -- directly observed, exact counts, cross-validated
between aggregated_statistics and independent recomputation from the 524 episodes):
- The distribution of failure stages, outcomes, scenarios, target types, and workarounds
 across the 524-episode sample (Sections 3, 4, 6).
- The exact frequency and outcome breakdown of specific action sequences in
 search_journey (Section 5).
- That the episode-level sample is 100% Play Store sourced, despite Reddit being 17.4% of
 the underlying document corpus.
- That the WORK scenario label does not describe occupational photo use, on direct
 inspection of its scenario_description text.
- That 79.4% of SEARCH actions have no captured query text, and that 79.6% of episodes
 record no workaround.

WHAT THE DATA SUGGESTS (INFERRED -- reasonable interpretation, not directly provable
from this data alone):
- That remembering a concrete, nameable object/subject correlates with better retrieval
 outcomes than remembering only situational context (Q2) -- a correlation, and possibly
 confounded by which kinds of episodes get written up as reviews at all.
- The forgotten-category semantic clustering (Section 3, Q3) -- our own grouping over an
 inconsistent free-text taxonomy.
- That app redesigns/reorganization are a causal trigger for the QUERY_UNDERSTANDING
 concentration in WORK-labeled episodes -- strongly suggested by the quotes themselves,
 but not independently verified against a release timeline.
- That the auto-generated-ephemeral-content pattern (H1) reflects an information-
 architecture gap rather than user inattention.
- That H5 (grief-related retrieval) is mechanistically a severity-weighted subset of H3
 rather than an independent problem.

WHAT THE DATA CANNOT ANSWER (UNKNOWN):
- The true population-level success or failure rate of Google Photos retrieval attempts;
 this sample is complaint-biased and single-channel and cannot be extrapolated to "X% of
 users."
- What users tried before writing the review, whether they eventually found the item
 after the review, or how they would describe the item completely unprompted (only a
 short evidence_quote fragment is available per episode, not a full transcript).
- Why 353/372 NOT_FOUND episodes (94.9%) show no recorded workaround -- true inaction vs.
 under-capture.
- Whether Reddit, App Store, or community-forum DIRECT_RETRIEVAL episodes (present in the
 document-level corpus but absent from this 524-episode sample) would change any pattern
 reported here.
- The 910-document (8.6%) gap between totalDocuments (10,641) and the sum of the four
 relevanceClassDistribution categories (9,731) -- unexplained by the data provided.
- Whether SEMANTIC_RETRIEVAL failures (H2) are caused by indexing lag, labeling quality,
 ranking, or genuine vocabulary mismatch -- this dataset shows the symptom, not the
 mechanism.
- Whether affected users in H3 (reorganization) eventually adapt and succeed later, since
 each episode is a single point-in-time complaint, not a longitudinal record.

====================================================================
10. PRIMARY RESEARCH GAPS -> INTERVIEW QUESTIONS
====================================================================

Secondary research (public reviews/discussions) cannot reliably establish: what
specifically triggered the search in the moment; how the user's memory of the item
degraded between when it was captured/created and when they searched; what, precisely,
they tried before giving up (workaround is null in 79.6% of episodes); whether they
eventually found the item through some other means after the review was written; how
they would describe the item completely unprompted, in their own words, before any
system feedback; and whether their mental model of "where things are" in Google Photos
matches the app's actual current structure.

Recommended questions for 5-6 user interviews:

1. "Think of the last time you searched for an old photo or video you couldn't
 immediately picture the location of. Walk me through it from the moment you decided
 to look, before you opened the app." (Surfaces the true memory-expression starting
 point, which this dataset cannot observe -- addresses the MEMORY_EXPRESSION gap.)

2. "What's the very first thing you typed or tapped? Why that, specifically, and not
 something else?" (Addresses the 79.4% missing-query-text gap in Q4.)

3. "When that didn't work, what did you do next -- and what did you decide NOT to try?"
 (Addresses the 79.6% no-workaround-recorded gap and the reformulation-vs-abandon
 question from Q5.)

4. "Did you eventually find it? If yes, how -- and how long did that take, roughly?" (No
 episode in this dataset tracks resolution beyond the review's writing moment.)

5. "Have you noticed Google Photos' layout, albums, or folders change over time? Do you
 feel like you know where things 'live' in the app right now?" (Directly tests H3's
 reorganization/mental-model hypothesis.)

6. "Has Google Photos ever made something for you automatically -- a collage, a
 highlight video, a 'memory' -- that you later couldn't find again? What did you do?"
 (Directly tests H1, the highest-priority hypothesis, which this dataset can only
 observe from unprompted complaints.)

7. "When you search using a word or name, and nothing comes up, what goes through your
 mind about why? Do you try a different word, or do something else entirely?"
 (Distinguishes genuine reformulation behavior from silent abandonment, addressing the
 2.5% reformulation-rate finding's ambiguity.)

8. "If you've ever needed to find a photo or video of someone you've lost -- a family
 member or pet -- what was that experience like?" (Only ask if volunteered or
 appropriate to raise; directly, carefully tests H5 without presuming the topic applies
 to the participant.)

9. "When you land in an album or date range where you're pretty sure the photo is, how
 do you actually scan for it? What makes that easy or hard?" (Tests H4's recognition/
 evaluation-friction hypothesis and helps separate bug-driven from cognition-driven
 friction, per the Section 8 contradiction.)

10. "How confident are you, generally, that if a photo exists in your library, Google
 Photos will eventually help you find it -- and has that confidence changed over
 time?" (Captures the trust/expectation dimension this transactional dataset cannot
 measure.)

====================================================================
11. RECOMMENDED SEGMENTS/PROBLEMS TO VALIDATE
====================================================================

1. Segment/scenario: Users who remember Google Photos auto-generated something
 (collage, memory video, stylized photo, highlight) via a push notification.
 Hypothesized root problem: no stable, browsable home for these creations once the
 notification is dismissed, forcing reliance on a one-time surface that isn't
 revisitable.
 Why it may affect the retrieval-success metric: this segment has the single highest
 observed failure rate in the dataset (86.7% NOT_FOUND vs. 71.0% baseline) among users
 who otherwise remember exactly what they're looking for -- a best-case scenario for
 improving the metric if the root cause is confirmed to be structural rather than
 behavioral.
 Supporting evidence: 45/524 episodes (8.6%), consistent quotes across HOBBY, EVENT,
 WORK-labeled, and OTHER scenarios.
 Missing evidence: whether a persistent surface for these creations already exists and
 is simply undiscovered vs. genuinely absent; true population frequency (Play Store
 sample only).
 What must be validated in interviews: whether users can relocate a known auto-
 generated creation unaided after time has passed, and where they instinctively look
 first.

2. Segment/scenario: Users issuing a short, concrete-subject search query (object,
 place, or person's name) that returns no relevant results despite the photo
 plausibly being indexed.
 Hypothesized root problem: a vocabulary/label mismatch or indexing/ranking gap between
 the user's plain-language term and the system's internal representation of the photo
 -- mechanism not distinguishable from this dataset.
 Why it may affect the retrieval-success metric: this is the single largest failure
 stage in the dataset (SEMANTIC_RETRIEVAL, 138/524, 26.3%) and directly represents the
 "remembers but can't retrieve" moment named in the business metric.
 Supporting evidence: 138/524 episodes; specific literal mismatches (water rail, rain,
 Amp, contact names); 17/524 explicit "AI/Gemini got worse" complaints.
 Missing evidence: whether failures are due to indexing lag, labeling quality, ranking,
 or genuine semantic mismatch; whether the "AI/Gemini" complaints reflect a specific,
 fixable regression or a persistent baseline limitation.
 What must be validated in interviews/instrumented testing: for a sample of real failed
 queries, whether the target photo is actually labeled/indexed with matching terms at
 all (this requires product telemetry, not just interviews, to fully resolve).

3. Segment/scenario: Users navigating Google Photos shortly after a redesign or
 reorganization event (the WORK-labeled proxy segment, most severe resolution rate in
 the dataset) who believe content is missing because they can't find it where it used
 to be.
 Hypothesized root problem: navigation and communication of structural changes do not
 preserve continuity with users' prior mental models, causing "missing" perception even
 when content still exists.
 Why it may affect the retrieval-success metric: this segment has the worst resolution
 rate of any scenario with adequate sample size (94% end NOT_FOUND or ABANDONED,
 n=52), and the failure mode (QUERY_UNDERSTANDING, not a fundamentally hard retrieval
 problem) is plausibly the most addressable of the five hypotheses without requiring
 search-model changes.
 Supporting evidence: 30/52 (57.7%) QUERY_UNDERSTANDING concentration within this
 segment vs. 22.1% corpus-wide; consistent "used to be able to find X, now can't" framing
 across album, folder, sharing, and face-grouping sub-patterns.
 Missing evidence: which specific releases/changes are implicated; whether affected
 users eventually adapt without intervention; how much of this is genuine navigation
 failure vs. preference-based complaint about a changed UI.
 What must be validated in interviews: whether users can rebuild an accurate mental
 model of "where things are now" within a reasonable time after a redesign, and what
 specifically would have preserved their orientation (e.g., a persistent search-first
 habit, as one contradictory data point already suggests, vs. improved in-place
 navigation cues).
